title: Mysterious Space Object Pulsed Every 62 Minutes Before Vanishing – ScienceAlert Discovery
body:
A fleeting burst of radio energy from the centre of our galaxy, timed to the minute and then disappearing without a trace, has reignited debate over the nature of exotic cosmic phenomena. In September 2002, a set of five ultra‑bright radio flares, each separated by exactly 77 minutes, were detected by the Parkes radio telescope in Australia. The signal, dubbed “GCRT J1745‑3009,” vanished after the fifth pulse, leaving astronomers scrambling to explain a source that behaved like nothing previously observed in the Milky Way’s crowded core.

The discovery was made while researchers were conducting a routine survey of the Galactic Centre at 330 MHz, a frequency well suited to probing dense, dust‑obscured regions. The transient source lit up the sky for a total of just over five hours, with each flare lasting roughly ten minutes before fading into the background. Its periodicity was astonishingly precise, matching the 77‑minute interval to within a fraction of a second—a regularity that suggested a rotating or orbiting system rather than a random burst. Yet, unlike known pulsars or magnetars, the emission was far more powerful and displayed a steep spectrum, indicating a different underlying mechanism.

Scientists have proposed several hypotheses, each with its own challenges. One leading idea is that the object could be a “radio magnetar,” a highly magnetised neutron star whose magnetic field twists and reconnects, releasing massive amounts of energy in the radio band. Magnetars are known to emit X‑ray and gamma‑ray flares, but a purely radio‑bright version would be unprecedented. Another possibility is that the source is a binary system containing a compact object—perhaps a white dwarf or neutron star—interacting with a dense cloud of plasma near the Galactic Centre. The regular interval could reflect the orbital period of the two bodies, with each encounter triggering a burst of synchrotron radiation.

A more exotic scenario involves a “propeller” mechanism, where a rapidly spinning neutron star ejects surrounding material at a rate that creates periodic radio outbursts. This model would require a fine‑tuned balance between spin rate, magnetic field strength, and accretion flow, conditions that are difficult to verify without additional observations. Some researchers have even floated the notion of a yet‑unknown class of objects, perhaps linked to the enigmatic fast radio bursts (FRBs) that have been observed extragalactically. The similarity lies in the brief, intense radio flashes, though FRBs typically occur on millisecond timescales and lack the regular cadence seen here.

The scarcity of data—only a single episode captured over a decade ago—poses a major obstacle. Follow‑up attempts using modern facilities such as the MeerKAT array in South Africa and the upgraded Very Large Array in New Mexico have yet to locate a repeat of the phenomenon, suggesting that the source may be transient by nature or that its activity window is extremely narrow. Nonetheless, the event has prompted a renewed focus on systematic monitoring of the Galactic Centre at low radio frequencies, a region historically difficult to survey due to interference from terrestrial sources and interstellar scattering.

If the mystery source reappears, it could provide a rare laboratory for testing theories of extreme magnetism, relativistic plasma, and the dynamics of matter under the influence of the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*. Even a single repeat detection would allow astronomers to pinpoint its position more accurately, measure its spectrum across a broader range, and perhaps catch associated high‑energy emissions. Until then, the 2002 flares remain a tantalising clue that the Milky Way still harbours hidden engines capable of producing remarkably ordered, yet fleeting, bursts of cosmic radio energy. Future surveys, bolstered by next‑generation telescopes such as the Square Kilometre Array, may finally unveil whether GCRT J1745‑3009 is a one‑off oddity or the first glimpse of a new astrophysical class.
